question: In 2016, what percentage of GWAS participants were of European ancestry? (Give a whole number and press Enter.)

answers.feedback: Right. 81% in 2016, down from 96% in 2009 - real progress, but still far from representative.
That was the 2009 figure. By 2016 it had fallen to 81%.
19% is the non-European share in 2016. The European share was 81%.
Look at the 2016 bar: European ancestry participants were 81% of samples.

question: Between 2009 and 2016 the number of GWAS samples grew about twentyfold. What happened to the representation gap?

answers.answer: The European share fell, but the absolute shortfall for other populations grew
answers.feedback: Right. A falling percentage of a much larger total can still mean a wider absolute gap.
European-ancestry participants still made up 81% of samples in 2016.

answers.answer: Representation got worse in percentage terms
answers.feedback: In percentage terms it improved, from 96% to 81%. The point is that the absolute shortfall grew anyway.
Native peoples showed no increase at all. Almost all the improvement came from Asian-ancestry cohorts.

question: Why do polygenic risk scores built in European cohorts lose accuracy in other populations?

answers.answer: Tag SNPs and their linkage disequilibrium with causal variants are population-specific
answers.feedback: Right. Accuracy falls roughly with genetic distance from the discovery cohort, so scores perform worst in African-ancestry individuals.

answers.answer: Other populations have no genetic contribution to the trait
answers.feedback: The genetic contribution exists. What does not transfer is the particular set of tag SNPs and weights.

answers.answer: The scores are calculated incorrectly outside Europe
answers.feedback: The arithmetic is the same. The problem is in the base data the weights came from.

answers.answer: Other populations have fewer SNPs in their genomes
answers.feedback: African populations in particular carry more genetic diversity, not less.
